summary: Defines an architecture for storing and retrieving digital versions of books, journals, photographs and similar material in a large organized digital library. It describes the document model used for the Cornell digital library project. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A plan for how a library keeps scanned books and pictures on computers so they can be stored and found again.

questions: how to store digital books and journals
how does cornell organize digital library documents
what is the cornell document architecture
how to structure digital books in a library
subtitle: How to organize scanned books and documents in a digital library

tldr.problem: Large digital libraries needed a standard way to organize and retrieve scanned books, journals, and images while preserving the structure and multiple views of physical documents.
tldr.mechanism: The Cornell architecture uses logical structure files to define document hierarchies and multiple views, physical reference files to map logical structures to actual image files, and data files containing the scanned images in various formats and resolutions.
tldr.outcome: This architecture enabled the Cornell Digital Library to store thousands of scanned documents while allowing users to browse at low resolution or print at high resolution, and to create documents that reference or incorporate parts of other documents.

today: RFC 1691 is Informational and documents the Cornell Digital Library architecture as of 1994. The project was later influential in digital library standards. The document architecture principles described here align with modern metadata standards like Dublin Core and continue to inform digital preservation practices, though the specific file formats and technologies have evolved significantly.

sections.title: The Cornell Digital Library Project
sections.content:
Starting in 1989, Cornell University and Xerox Corporation partnered to develop methods for digitally preserving library materials. Xerox developed the CLASS (College Library Access and Storage System), while Cornell created software for network access. A key challenge was storing both low-resolution images for browsing over the network and high-resolution images for printing, along with defining internal document structures that users could navigate.

Cornell later defined its own document architecture, building on lessons learned from the CLASS project. This RFC documents that architecture, which the university continues to use for organizing its digital library collections. The design preserves the logical structure of physical books—title pages, table of contents, chapters, indexes—while storing them as collections of scanned image files.
sections.eli5: A university wanted to scan books and store them on computers. They needed a way to organize the scanned pages so people could browse quickly on the internet and also print high-quality copies.

sections.title: Document Structure: Logical and Physical
sections.content:
A digital document in the Cornell architecture consists of three parts: the logical structure, the physical references, and the data files. The logical structure is a tree that defines how the document is organized. Just as a physical book has a title page, table of contents, chapters, and an index, a digital document has a logical structure that preserves these hierarchies and relationships. A special structure called PAGES lists all pages in order, but other views may organize the same document differently—by chapters, by subject, or by other logical groupings.

Physical references map the logical structure to the actual files. Where multiple file formats exist for a single page—such as high-resolution TIFF, low-resolution thumbnail, and OCR text—these are linked together so they can be accessed based on use case. The data files themselves contain the actual image data, text, or other content. Any file format can be used: TIFF images, ASCII text, PostScript, or others.
sections.eli5: A digital book has two sets of instructions. One says what the book looks like (title, chapters, etc.). The other says where the actual scanned pages are stored. The actual pages can exist in different qualities (big or small) and different formats.

sections.title: The Three-Part Document Model
sections.content:
The Physical References File connects logical documents to physical files. It contains two types of lines: Document Object lines and Data Object lines. Document Object lines describe master documents (created by scanning) and reference documents (incorporating parts of other documents). A Master Document Object is created for original content; Reference Document Objects are created when a document includes material from other documents, possibly on different servers.

Data Object lines specify the actual files, including their location, type, and resolution. File types are numbered: 1 for high-resolution TIFF (600 dpi), 2 for thumbnail TIFF, 3 for OCR text output, 4 for notes, 5 for other, and 6 for medium-resolution TIFF (300 dpi). The tuple of library ID, collection ID, document ID, file type, and file reference uniquely identifies any file in the system.

The Logical Structure File defines how the document is organized. It uses a tree format where each structure line has a parent, a sequence number, a name or label, and counts of logical and physical children. This allows creating multiple views of the same document—one person might navigate by chapter, while another navigates by author or subject, all using the same underlying data files.
sections.eli5: The storage system uses index cards to track where every page lives and what format it is in. Another index describes how the book is organized—which pages come first, which ones are chapters, and which are the index.

sections.title: Flexible Storage and Multiple Views
sections.content:
The architecture supports flexible directory hierarchies. Rather than mandating a fixed structure, the system allows different organizations optimized for different purposes. One approach stores everything by library, then collection, then document, then file type. Another stores by file type first, then collection, then document. This flexibility lets administrators choose storage strategies that match their performance and access patterns.

For example, low-resolution images can be stored on fast magnetic disk for quick browsing, while high-resolution images go to slower, less expensive storage. This separation also enables different access controls: users might browse low-resolution images via FTP or Gopher, while high-resolution images remain restricted. The architecture also supports documents composed of references to other documents, allowing logical composition without physical duplication, and supports documents distributed across multiple networked servers.
sections.eli5: The system can organize files in different ways depending on what works best. Computers can quickly show small pictures for browsing, and separately store big, detailed pictures for printing. Libraries can also link documents together without copying all the files.

sections.title: Implementation and File Locating
sections.content:
The architecture uses a file locator program to translate between logical identifiers and actual file system paths. Each level of the directory hierarchy contains an INFO file describing the organization of lower levels. When opening a library, collection, or document, the file locator reads these files while navigating the directory structure.

The tuple consisting of library ID, collection ID, document ID, file type, and file reference guarantees location of any file. Because the directory hierarchy has a flexible nature matching UNIX file systems, the implementation can optimize storage across different physical disk systems. This allows complete copies of collections to be mounted on different file systems for performance, and enables storing different file types (high-resolution versus thumbnail) on media with different cost and performance characteristics.
sections.eli5: A program looks up where files are actually stored by reading a series of guidebooks in the directory tree. Any file can be found by giving its library, collection, document, type, and reference number.
